overview: Pandas is the workhorse of data manipulation in Python. This module covers the essential operations: reading data, indexing and filtering, grouping and aggregation, merging datasets, and handling missing data.
Everything converges from NumPy: arrays become vectors and matrices, shapes have dimensional meaning, broadcasting enables efficient operations. Machine Learning = Linear Algebra executed at scale.

topics.title: Linear Algebra with NumPy
theory: In NumPy: 1D arrays are vectors, 2D arrays are matrices. But interpretation matters: (n,) ≠ (n, 1) ≠ (1, n). Shape defines semantics — always inspect shapes before operations.

Dot product (np.dot(a, b)) measures similarity, projection, and contribution weighting. Used in linear models, cosine similarity, and attention mechanisms. Matrix multiplication (X @ W) is the engine of linear models — inner dimensions must match.
Transpose (X.T) is required for normal equations, covariance matrices, and gradient calculations. It swaps rows and columns — a semantic change, not just cosmetic.

For solving linear systems, prefer np.linalg.solve(A, b) over np.linalg.inv(A) @ b — it's more stable, faster, and numerically safer. Matrix rank tells you how much independent information exists and whether solutions are unique.

Eigenvalues/eigenvectors (np.linalg.eig(A)) measure directional importance and define principal directions. SVD (np.linalg.svd) enables dimensionality reduction, noise removal, and low-rank approximation. PCA = SVD on centered data.
visualIntuition: Geometry of linear algebra in ML: Data as points in space, weights as directions, dot product as projection, matrix multiplication as space transformation. Training a model means rotating and scaling space until patterns align.
visualSuggestions: Matrix multiplication as space transformation animation
SVD decomposition showing rotate → scale → rotate

code.content:
import numpy as np

v = np.array([1, 2, 3])      # vector
X = np.array([[1, 2],
              [3, 4]])       # matrix

# Dot product
print(np.dot(v, v))  # 14

# Matrix multiplication
W = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])
print(X @ W)

# Transpose
print(X.T)

code.description: Solving linear systems and linear regression
code.content:
import numpy as np

# Linear regression in pure NumPy
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
y = np.array([2, 4, 5, 4, 5])

# Design matrix with bias column
X = np.c_[np.ones(len(x)), x]

# Solve using normal equation (stable version)
theta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
print("Intercept and slope:", theta)

topics.title: Reading & Writing Data
theory: How datasets enter your workflow matters. Formats (CSV, Excel, JSON, Parquet) are not equivalent — they influence structure and types differently.
Schema inference can be wrong. Explicit dtypes prevent downstream bugs. If data is wrong at load time, everything after is compromised.
This topic teaches how formats influence structure, how data integrity can be lost at ingestion, and why explicit type specification matters.
visualIntuition: Pipeline view: Raw Files → Read & Validate → Select & Filter → Group & Summarize → Merge Context → Handle Missingness → Clean Dataset → ML/Visualization
visualSuggestions: Format comparison showing same data in CSV vs JSON vs Parquet

code.content:
import pandas as pd

# Read with explicit dtypes
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', dtype={'age': 'int32', 'income': 'float64'})

# Specify date parsing
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv', parse_dates=['date_column'])

topics.title: Indexing & Filtering
theory: Difference between label-based (loc) and position-based (iloc) access is critical. Pandas forces explicit intent to prevent silent mistakes.
Boolean masks provide vectorized filtering — replacing loops with declarative expressions. Index alignment is more important than row numbers.
Selection is a semantic operation, not a positional one. This mindset prevents many common bugs.
visualIntuition: Boolean mask visualization: condition creates True/False array, which filters rows when applied to DataFrame.
visualSuggestions: loc vs iloc comparison with index labels

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3], 'B': [4, 5, 6]}, index=['x', 'y', 'z'])

# Label-based (use column names and index labels)
print(df.loc['x', 'A'])

# Position-based (use integer positions)
print(df.iloc[0, 0])

# Boolean filtering
filtered = df[df['A'] > 1]
print(filtered)

topics.title: GroupBy & Aggregation
theory: Split → Apply → Combine pattern is the heart of analytics. Groups define context, aggregations define questions, results define insight.
GroupBy is asking the same question repeatedly for different slices of data. This turns rows into insights.
visualIntuition: Split-Apply-Combine diagram: DataFrame splits into groups, function applies to each, results combine into summary table.
visualSuggestions: Multiple aggregation functions on same group

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'category': ['A', 'A', 'B', 'B'],
    'value': [10, 20, 30, 40]
})

# Basic groupby
print(df.groupby('category')['value'].mean())

# Multiple aggregations
print(df.groupby('category')['value'].agg(['mean', 'sum', 'count']))

topics.title: Merging & Joining
theory: Reconstructing reality from fragmented data requires understanding how relational data combines. Keys matter more than rows — wrong join = wrong dataset.
A join is a claim about how two datasets relate. Cardinality awareness is critical to avoid duplication and data leakage.
Join types: inner (matching only), left (keep all left), right (keep all right), outer (keep all).
visualIntuition: Venn diagram showing different join types and which rows are kept from each table.
visualSuggestions: Join type comparison with same example data
Cardinality warning when one-to-many becomes many-to-many

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df1 = pd.DataFrame({'key': ['A', 'B', 'C'], 'value1': [1, 2, 3]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'key': ['A', 'B', 'D'], 'value2': [4, 5, 6]})

# Inner join (matching keys only)
inner = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='key', how='inner')

# Left join (keep all from left)
left = pd.merge(df1, df2, on='key', how='left')

print("Inner:\n", inner)
print("Left:\n", left)

topics.title: Handling Missing Data
theory: Missingness is information, not error. Missing ≠ zero, missing ≠ bug. How you handle missing data encodes assumptions.
Dropping vs imputing has consequences. NaNs propagate intentionally in Pandas. Imputation strategy depends on whether data is MCAR, MAR, or MNAR.
Common anti-patterns: chaining operations without inspecting output, relying on default behavior, ignoring index alignment, joining without checking row counts, dropping NaNs blindly.
visualIntuition: Distribution comparison: original data vs after dropping missing vs after mean imputation — showing how imputation shrinks variance.
visualSuggestions: Missing pattern visualization (matrix of NaN locations)

code.content:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, np.nan, 3], 'B': [4, 5, np.nan]})

# Check for missing
print(df.isna().sum())

# Drop rows with any missing
print(df.dropna())

# Fill with median
print(df.fillna(df.median()))

# Create missingness indicator
df['A_missing'] = df['A'].isna().astype(int)
